# num-traits

Numeric traits for generic mathematics in Rust.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature. Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
 = false
# features = ["libm"]    # <--- Uncomment if you wish to use `Float` and `Real` without `std`
```
The `Float` and `Real` traits are only available when either `std` or `libm` is enabled.

The `FloatCore` trait is always available.  `MulAdd` and `MulAddAssign` for `f32`
and `f64` also require `std` or `libm`, as do implementations of signed and floating-
point exponents in `Pow`.

# num 0.4.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num/0.4.1

# num

A collection of numeric types and traits for Rust.

This includes new types for big integers, rationals (aka fractions), and complex numbers,
new traits for generic programming on numeric properties like `Integer`,
and generic range iterators.

`num` is a meta-crate, re-exporting items from these sub-crates:

| Repository | Crate | Documentation |
|---|---|---|
| `num-bigint` | ||
| `num-complex` | ||
| `num-integer` | ||
| `num-iter` | ||
| `num-rational` | ||
| `num-traits` | ||
| ( )`num-derive` |

Note: `num-derive` is listed here for reference, but it's not directly included
in `num`.  This is a `proc-macro` crate for deriving some of `num`'s traits.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature. Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
 = false
```
The `num-bigint` crate requires the `std` feature, or the `alloc` feature may
be used instead with Rust 1.36 and later. Other sub-crates may also have
limited functionality when used without `std`.

The `libm` feature uses pure-Rust floating point implementations in `no_std`
builds, enabling the `Float` trait and related `Complex` methods.

The `rand` feature enables randomization traits in `num-bigint` and
`num-complex`.

The `serde` feature enables serialization for types in `num-bigint`,
`num-complex`, and `num-rational`.

The `num` meta-crate no longer supports features to toggle the inclusion of
the individual sub-crates.  If you need such control, you are recommended to
directly depend on your required crates instead.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num` crate as a whole is tested for rustc 1.31 and greater.

The `num-traits`, `num-integer`, and `num-iter` crates are individually tested
for rustc 1.8 and greater, if you require such older compatibility.

## License

Licensed under either of

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

---

The `rand` feature enables randomization traits in `num-bigint` and
`num-complex`.

The `serde` feature enables serialization for types in `num-bigint`,
`num-complex`, and `num-rational`.

The `num` meta-crate no longer supports features to toggle the inclusion of
the individual sub-crates.  If you need such control, you are recommended to
directly depend on your required crates instead.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num` crate as a whole is tested for rustc 1.31 and greater.

The `num-traits`, `num-integer`, and `num-iter` crates are individually tested
for rustc 1.8 and greater, if you require such older compatibility.

---

# num 0.2.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num/0.2.1

# num

A collection of numeric types and traits for Rust.

This includes new types for big integers, rationals (aka fractions), and complex numbers,
new traits for generic programming on numeric properties like `Integer`,
and generic range iterators.

`num` is a meta-crate, re-exporting items from these sub-crates:

| Repository | Crate | Documentation |
|---|---|---|
| `num-bigint` | ||
| `num-complex` | ||
| `num-integer` | ||
| `num-iter` | ||
| `num-rational` | ||
| `num-traits` | ||
| ( )`num-derive` |

Note: `num-derive` is listed here for reference, but it's not directly included
in `num`.  This is a `proc-macro` crate for deriving some of `num`'s traits.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
and this to your crate root:

```
extern crate num;
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature. Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
 = false
```
The `num-bigint` crate is only available when `std` is enabled, and the other
sub-crates may have limited functionality when used without `std`.

Implementations for `i128` and `u128` are only available with Rust 1.26 and
later.  The build script automatically detects this, but you can make it
mandatory by enabling the `i128` crate feature.

The `rand` feature enables randomization traits in `num-bigint` and
`num-complex`.

The `serde` feature enables serialization for types in `num-bigint`,
`num-complex`, and `num-rational`.

The `num` meta-crate no longer supports features to toggle the inclusion of
the individual sub-crates.  If you need such control, you are recommended to
directly depend on your required crates instead.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num` crate as a whole is tested for rustc 1.15 and greater.

The `num-traits`, `num-integer`, and `num-iter` crates are individually tested
for rustc 1.8 and greater, if you require such older compatibility.

---

# num - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num

## Expand description

A collection of numeric types and traits for Rust.

This includes new types for big integers, rationals, and complex numbers,
new traits for generic programming on numeric properties like `Integer`,
and generic range iterators.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This example uses the BigRational type and [Newton’s method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methods_of_computing_square_roots#Babylonian_method) to
approximate a square root to arbitrary precision:

```
use num::FromPrimitive;
use num::bigint::BigInt;
use num::rational::{Ratio, BigRational};
fn approx_sqrt(number: u64, iterations: usize) -> BigRational {
    let start: Ratio<BigInt> = Ratio::from_integer(FromPrimitive::from_u64(number).unwrap());
    let mut approx = start.clone();
    for _ in 0..iterations {
        approx = (&approx + (&start / &approx)) /
            Ratio::from_integer(FromPrimitive::from_u64(2).unwrap());
    }
    approx
}
fn main() {
    println!("{}", approx_sqrt(10, 4)); // prints 4057691201/1283082416
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

The `num` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)
- A big signed integer type.
- [BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)
- A big unsigned integer type.
- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- A complex number in Cartesian form.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Bounded](https://docs.rs/trait.Bounded.html)
- Numbers which have upper and lower bounds
- [Checked](https://docs.rs/trait.CheckedAdd.html)- Add
- Performs addition that returns `None`instead of wrapping around on overflow.
- [Checked](https://docs.rs/trait.CheckedDiv.html)- Div
- Performs division that returns `None`instead of panicking on division by zero and instead of wrapping around on underflow and overflow.
- [Checked](https://docs.rs/trait.CheckedMul.html)- Mul
- Performs multiplication that returns `None`instead of wrapping around on underflow or overflow.
- [Checked](https://docs.rs/trait.CheckedSub.html)- Sub
- Performs subtraction that returns `None`instead of wrapping around on underflow.
- [Float](https://docs.rs/trait.Float.html)
- Generic trait for floating point numbers
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromPrimitive.html)- Primitive
- A generic trait for converting a number to a value.
- [Integer](https://docs.rs/trait.Integer.html)
- [Num](https://docs.rs/trait.Num.html)
- The base trait for numeric types, covering `0`and`1`values, comparisons, basic numeric operations, and string conversion.
- [NumCast](https://docs.rs/trait.NumCast.html)
- An interface for casting between machine scalars.
- [One](https://docs.rs/trait.One.html)
- Defines a multiplicative identity element for `Self`.
- [PrimInt](https://docs.rs/trait.PrimInt.html)
- Generic trait for primitive integers.
- [Saturating](https://docs.rs/trait.Saturating.html)
- Saturating math operations. Deprecated, use `SaturatingAdd`,`SaturatingSub`and`SaturatingMul`instead.
- [Signed](https://docs.rs/trait.Signed.html)
- Useful functions for signed numbers (i.e. numbers that can be negative).
- [ToPrimitive](https://docs.rs/trait.ToPrimitive.html)
- A generic trait for converting a value to a number.
- [Unsigned](https://docs.rs/trait.Unsigned.html)
- A trait for values which cannot be negative
- [Zero](https://docs.rs/trait.Zero.html)
- Defines an additive identity element for `Self`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [abs](https://docs.rs/fn.abs.html)
- Computes the absolute value.
- [abs_sub](https://docs.rs/fn.abs_sub.html)
- The positive difference of two numbers.
- [cast](https://docs.rs/fn.cast.html)
- Cast from one machine scalar to another.
- [checked_](https://docs.rs/fn.checked_pow.html)- pow
- Raises a value to the power of exp, returning `None`if an overflow occurred.
- [clamp](https://docs.rs/fn.clamp.html)
- A value bounded by a minimum and a maximum
- [one](https://docs.rs/fn.one.html)
- Returns the multiplicative identity, `1`.
- [pow](https://docs.rs/fn.pow.html)
- Raises a value to the power of exp, using exponentiation by squaring.
- [range](https://docs.rs/fn.range.html)
- Returns an iterator over the given range [start, stop) (that is, starting at start (inclusive), and ending at stop (exclusive)).
- [range_](https://docs.rs/fn.range_inclusive.html)- inclusive
- Return an iterator over the range [start, stop]
- [range_](https://docs.rs/fn.range_step.html)- step
- Return an iterator over the range [start, stop) by `step`. It handles overflow by stopping.
- [range_](https://docs.rs/fn.range_step_inclusive.html)- step_ - inclusive
- Return an iterator over the range [start, stop] by `step`. It handles overflow by stopping.
- [signum](https://docs.rs/fn.signum.html)
- Returns the sign of the number.
- [zero](https://docs.rs/fn.zero.html)
- Returns the additive identity, `0`.

# num_bigint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-bigint/

## Expand description

Big Integer Types for Rust

- A `BigUint`
- A `BigInt``BigUint``Sign`

Common numerical operations are overloaded, so we can treat them the same way we treat other numbers.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_bigint::BigUint;
use num_traits::One;
// Calculate large fibonacci numbers.
fn fib(n: usize) -> BigUint {
    let mut f0 = BigUint::ZERO;
    let mut f1 = BigUint::one();
    for _ in 0..n {
        let f2 = f0 + &f1;
        f0 = f1;
        f1 = f2;
    }
    f0
}
// This is a very large number.
println!("fib(1000) = {}", fib(1000));
```
It’s easy to generate large random numbers:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use num_bigint::{ToBigInt, RandBigInt};
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let a = rng.gen_bigint(1000);
let low = -10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let high = 10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let b = rng.gen_bigint_range(&low, &high);
// Probably an even larger number.
println!("{}", a * b);
```
See the “Features” section for instructions for enabling random number generation.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

The `std` crate feature is enabled by default, which enables [ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html)
implementations and some internal use of floating point approximations. This can be disabled by
depending on

`num-bigint` with `default-features = false`. Either way, the `alloc` crate is
always required for heap allocation of the `BigInt`/`BigUint` digits.[§](https://docs.rs#random-generation)Random Generation

`num-bigint` supports the generation of random big integers when the `rand`
feature is enabled. To enable it include rand as

```
rand = "0.8"
num-bigint = { version = "0.4", features = ["rand"] }
```
Note that you must use the version of `rand` that `num-bigint` is compatible
with: `0.8`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arbitrary-big-integers)Arbitrary Big Integers

`num-bigint` supports `arbitrary` and `quickcheck` features to implement
[ arbitrary::Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/1.4.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html) and

[, respectively, for both](https://docs.rs/quickcheck/1.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/quickcheck/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`quickcheck::Arbitrary``BigInt` and
`BigUint`. These are useful for fuzzing and other forms of randomized testing.[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

The `serde` feature adds implementations of [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) and

[for both](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize``BigInt` and `BigUint`. Their serialized data is
generated portably, regardless of platform differences like the internal digit size.[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

The `num-bigint` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)
- A big signed integer type.
- [BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)
- A big unsigned integer type.
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/struct.ParseBigIntError.html)- BigInt - Error

- A random distribution for `BigUint``BigInt`
- [TryFrom](https://docs.rs/struct.TryFromBigIntError.html)- BigInt - Error
- The error type returned when a checked conversion regarding big integer fails.
- [U32Digits](https://docs.rs/struct.U32Digits.html)
- An iterator of `u32`digits representation of a`BigUint`or`BigInt`, ordered least significant digit first.
- [U64Digits](https://docs.rs/struct.U64Digits.html)
- An iterator of `u64`digits representation of a`BigUint`or`BigInt`, ordered least significant digit first.
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformBigInt.html)- BigInt - `rand`
- The back-end implementing rand’s `UniformSampler``BigInt`

- `pub use crate::pow::`- [Pow](https://docs.rs/pow/trait.Pow.html);
- `pub use crate::sign::`- [abs](https://docs.rs/sign/fn.abs.html);
- `pub use crate::sign::`- [abs_sub](https://docs.rs/sign/fn.abs_sub.html);
- `pub use crate::sign::`- [signum](https://docs.rs/sign/fn.signum.html);
- `pub use crate::sign::`- [Signed](https://docs.rs/sign/trait.Signed.html);
- `pub use crate::sign::`- [Unsigned](https://docs.rs/sign/trait.Unsigned.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Num](https://docs.rs/trait.Num.html)
- The base trait for numeric types, covering `0`and`1`values, comparisons, basic numeric operations, and string conversion.
- [NumAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.NumAssign.html)
- The trait for `Num`types which also implement assignment operators.
- [NumAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.NumAssignOps.html)- Ops
- Generic trait for types implementing numeric assignment operators (like `+=`).
- [NumAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.NumAssignRef.html)- Ref
- The trait for `NumAssign`types which also implement assignment operations taking the second operand by reference.
- [NumOps](https://docs.rs/trait.NumOps.html)
- Generic trait for types implementing basic numeric operations
- [NumRef](https://docs.rs/trait.NumRef.html)
- The trait for `Num`types which also implement numeric operations taking the second operand by reference.
- [RefNum](https://docs.rs/trait.RefNum.html)
- The trait for `Num`references which implement numeric operations, taking the second operand either by value or by reference.

# num_derive - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-derive/

## Expand description

Procedural macros to derive numeric traits in Rust.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
num-traits = "0.2"
num-derive = "0.3"
```
Then you can derive traits on your own types:

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate num_derive;
#[derive(FromPrimitive, ToPrimitive)]
enum Color {
    Red,
    Blue,
    Green,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#explicit-import)Explicit import

By default the `num_derive` procedural macros assume that the
`num_traits` crate is a direct dependency. If `num_traits` is instead
a transitive dependency, the `num_traits` helper attribute can be
used to tell `num_derive` to use a specific identifier for its imports.

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate num_derive;
// Lets pretend this is a transitive dependency from another crate
// reexported as `some_other_ident`.
extern crate num_traits as some_other_ident;
#[derive(FromPrimitive, ToPrimitive)]
#[num_traits = "some_other_ident"]
enum Color {
    Red,
    Blue,
    Green,
}
```
## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Float](https://docs.rs/derive.Float.html)
- Derives `num_traits::Float``Float`.
- [From](https://docs.rs/derive.FromPrimitive.html)- Primitive
- Derives `num_traits::FromPrimitive`
- [Num](https://docs.rs/derive.Num.html)
- Derives `num_traits::Num``Num`.
- [NumCast](https://docs.rs/derive.NumCast.html)
- Derives `num_traits::NumCast``NumCast`.
- [NumOps](https://docs.rs/derive.NumOps.html)
- Derives `num_traits::NumOps``NumOps`.
- [One](https://docs.rs/derive.One.html)
- Derives `num_traits::One``One`.
- [Signed](https://docs.rs/derive.Signed.html)
- Derives `num_traits::Signed``Signed`.
- [ToPrimitive](https://docs.rs/derive.ToPrimitive.html)
- Derives `num_traits::ToPrimitive`
- [Unsigned](https://docs.rs/derive.Unsigned.html)
- Derives `num_traits::Unsigned``Unsigned`.
- [Zero](https://docs.rs/derive.Zero.html)
- Derives `num_traits::Zero``Zero`.

# num 0.4.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num/latest/source/README.md

```
[![crate](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/num.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/num)
[![documentation](https://docs.rs/num/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/num)
[![minimum rustc 1.60](https://img.shields.io/badge/rustc-1.60+-red.svg)](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2495-min-rust-version.html)
[![build status](https://github.com/rust-num/num/workflows/master/badge.svg)](https://github.com/rust-num/num/actions)
A collection of numeric types and traits for Rust.
This includes new types for big integers, rationals (aka fractions), and complex numbers,
new traits for generic programming on numeric properties like `Integer`,
and generic range iterators.
`num` is a meta-crate, re-exporting items from these sub-crates:
Note: `num-derive` is listed here for reference, but it's not directly included
in `num`.  This is a `proc-macro` crate for deriving some of `num`'s traits.
Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:
```toml
[dependencies]
num = "0.4"
```
This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature. Use this in `Cargo.toml`:
```toml
[dependencies.num]
version = "0.4"
default-features = false
```
The `num-bigint` crate requires the `std` feature, or the `alloc` feature may
be used instead with Rust 1.36 and later. Other sub-crates may also have
limited functionality when used without `std`.
The `libm` feature uses pure-Rust floating point implementations in `no_std`
builds, enabling the `Float` trait and related `Complex` methods.
The `rand` feature enables randomization traits in `num-bigint` and
`num-complex`.
The `serde` feature enables serialization for types in `num-bigint`,
`num-complex`, and `num-rational`.
The `num` meta-crate no longer supports features to toggle the inclusion of
the individual sub-crates.  If you need such control, you are recommended to
directly depend on your required crates instead.
Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](RELEASES.md).
The `num` crate as a whole is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.
The `num-traits`, `num-integer`, and `num-iter` crates are individually tested
for rustc 1.8 and greater, if you require such older compatibility.
Licensed under either of
 *  *
at your option.
Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted
for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be
dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.
```

# num-bigint 0.4.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-bigint/0.4.6

# num-bigint

Big integer types for Rust, `BigInt` and `BigUint`.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
## Features

The `std` crate feature is enabled by default, and is mandatory before Rust
1.36 and the stabilized `alloc` crate.  If you depend on `num-bigint` with
`default-features = false`, you must manually enable the `std` feature yourself
if your compiler is not new enough.

### Random Generation

`num-bigint` supports the generation of random big integers when the `rand`
feature is enabled. To enable it include rand as

```
 = "0.8"
 = {  = "0.4",  = ["rand"] }
```
Note that you must use the version of `rand` that `num-bigint` is compatible
with: `0.8`.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-bigint` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## Alternatives

While `num-bigint` strives for good performance in pure Rust code, other
crates may offer better performance with different trade-offs.  The following
table offers a brief comparison to a few alternatives.

| Crate | License | Min rustc | Implementation | Features |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `num-bigint` | MIT/Apache-2.0 | 1.60 | pure rust | dynamic width, number theoretical functions |
| `awint` | MIT/Apache-2.0 | 1.66 | pure rust | fixed width, heap or stack, concatenation macros |
| `bnum` | MIT/Apache-2.0 | 1.65 | pure rust | fixed width, parity with Rust primitives including floats |
| `crypto-bigint` | MIT/Apache-2.0 | 1.73 | pure rust | fixed width, stack only |
| `ibig` | MIT/Apache-2.0 | 1.49 | pure rust | dynamic width, number theoretical functions |
| `rug` | LGPL-3.0+ | 1.65 | bundles [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)via`gmp-mpfr-sys` | all the features of GMP, MPFR, and MPC |

## License

Licensed under either of

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

---

# num-bigint 0.4.6 - Docs.rs

#
                    num-bigint 0.4.6

                Big integer implementation for Rust

# arbitrary - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arbitrary/^1/

## Expand description

The `Arbitrary` trait crate.

This trait provides an [ Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html) trait to
produce well-typed, structured values, from raw, byte buffers. It is
generally intended to be used with fuzzers like AFL or libFuzzer. See the

[trait’s documentation for details on automatically deriving, implementing, and/or using the trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`Arbitrary`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [size_](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html)- hint
- Utilities for working with and combining the results of
`Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [unstructured](https://docs.rs/unstructured/index.html)
- Wrappers around raw, unstructured bytes.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [MaxRecursion](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)- Reached
- Error indicating that the maximum recursion depth has been reached while calculating `Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)
- A source of unstructured data.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- An enumeration of buffer creation errors

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- Generate arbitrary structured values from raw, unstructured data.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A `Result`with the error type fixed as`arbitrary::Error`.

---

# num_traits - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-traits/^0.2.18/

## Expand description

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::bounds::`- [Bounded](https://docs.rs/bounds/trait.Bounded.html);
- `pub use crate::float::`- [Float](https://docs.rs/float/trait.Float.html);
- `pub use crate::float::`- [FloatConst](https://docs.rs/float/trait.FloatConst.html);
- `pub use crate::cast::`- [cast](https://docs.rs/cast/fn.cast.html);
- `pub use crate::cast::`- [AsPrimitive](https://docs.rs/cast/trait.AsPrimitive.html);

# quickcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quickcheck/^1/

## Expand description

This crate is a port of
[Haskell’s QuickCheck](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/QuickCheck).

QuickCheck is a library for random testing of program properties. The programmer provides a specification of the program, in the form of properties which functions should satisfy, and QuickCheck then tests that the properties hold in a large number of randomly generated cases.

For detailed examples, please see the
[README](https://github.com/BurntSushi/quickcheck).

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

In general, this crate considers the `Arbitrary` implementations provided as
implementation details. Strategies may or may not change over time, which may
cause new test failures, presumably due to the discovery of new bugs due to a
new kind of witness being generated. These sorts of changes may happen in
semver compatible releases.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/macro.quickcheck.html)
- A macro for writing quickcheck tests.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Gen](https://docs.rs/struct.Gen.html)
- `Gen`represents a PRNG.
- [NoShrink](https://docs.rs/struct.NoShrink.html)
- Wrapper for disabling shrinking for an Arbitrary
- [Quick](https://docs.rs/struct.QuickCheck.html)- Check
- The main `QuickCheck`type for setting configuration and running`QuickCheck`.
- [Test](https://docs.rs/struct.TestResult.html)- Result
- Describes the status of a single instance of a test.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- `Arbitrary`describes types whose values can be randomly generated and shrunk.
- [Testable](https://docs.rs/trait.Testable.html)
- `Testable`describes types (e.g., a function) whose values can be tested.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [empty_](https://docs.rs/fn.empty_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with zero elements.
- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/fn.quickcheck.html)
- Convenience function for running `QuickCheck`.
- [single_](https://docs.rs/fn.single_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with a single element.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [distributions](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)
- Generating random samples from probability distributions
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Convenience re-export of common members
- [rngs](https://docs.rs/rngs/index.html)
- Random number generators and adapters
- [seq](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)
- Sequence-related functionality

- Error type of random number generators

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/trait.CryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait used to indicate that an `RngCore``BlockRngCore`
- [Fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Fill.html)
- Types which may be filled with random data
- [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)
- An automatically-implemented extension trait on `RngCore`
- [RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html)
- The core of a random number generator.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [random](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html)- `std`and- `std_rng`
- Generates a random value using the thread-local random number generator.
- [thread_](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)- rng - `std`and- `std_rng`
- Retrieve the lazily-initialized thread-local random number generator,
seeded by the system. Intended to be used in method chaining style,
e.g. `thread_rng().gen::<i32>()`, or cached locally, e.g.`let mut rng = thread_rng();`. Invoked by the`Default`trait, making`ThreadRng::default()`equivalent.

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# num_bigint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-bigint/0.4.6/target-redirect/num_bigint/

## Expand description

Big Integer Types for Rust

- A `BigUint`
- A `BigInt``BigUint``Sign`

Common numerical operations are overloaded, so we can treat them the same way we treat other numbers.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_bigint::BigUint;
use num_traits::One;
// Calculate large fibonacci numbers.
fn fib(n: usize) -> BigUint {
    let mut f0 = BigUint::ZERO;
    let mut f1 = BigUint::one();
    for _ in 0..n {
        let f2 = f0 + &f1;
        f0 = f1;
        f1 = f2;
    }
    f0
}
// This is a very large number.
println!("fib(1000) = {}", fib(1000));
```
It’s easy to generate large random numbers:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use num_bigint::{ToBigInt, RandBigInt};
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let a = rng.gen_bigint(1000);
let low = -10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let high = 10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let b = rng.gen_bigint_range(&low, &high);
// Probably an even larger number.
println!("{}", a * b);
```
See the “Features” section for instructions for enabling random number generation.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

The `std` crate feature is enabled by default, which enables [ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html)
implementations and some internal use of floating point approximations. This can be disabled by
depending on

`num-bigint` with `default-features = false`. Either way, the `alloc` crate is
always required for heap allocation of the `BigInt`/`BigUint` digits.[§](https://docs.rs#random-generation)Random Generation

`num-bigint` supports the generation of random big integers when the `rand`
feature is enabled. To enable it include rand as

```
rand = "0.8"
num-bigint = { version = "0.4", features = ["rand"] }
```
Note that you must use the version of `rand` that `num-bigint` is compatible
with: `0.8`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arbitrary-big-integers)Arbitrary Big Integers

`num-bigint` supports `arbitrary` and `quickcheck` features to implement
[ arbitrary::Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/1.4.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html) and

[, respectively, for both](https://docs.rs/quickcheck/1.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/quickcheck/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`quickcheck::Arbitrary``BigInt` and
`BigUint`. These are useful for fuzzing and other forms of randomized testing.[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

The `serde` feature adds implementations of [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) and

[for both](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize``BigInt` and `BigUint`. Their serialized data is
generated portably, regardless of platform differences like the internal digit size.[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

The `num-bigint` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)
- A big signed integer type.
- [BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)
- A big unsigned integer type.
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/struct.ParseBigIntError.html)- BigInt - Error
- [Random](https://docs.rs/struct.RandomBits.html)- Bits - `rand`
- A random distribution for `BigUint``BigInt`
- [TryFrom](https://docs.rs/struct.TryFromBigIntError.html)- BigInt - Error
- The error type returned when a checked conversion regarding big integer fails.
- [U32Digits](https://docs.rs/struct.U32Digits.html)
- An iterator of `u32`digits representation of a`BigUint`or`BigInt`, ordered least significant digit first.
- [U64Digits](https://docs.rs/struct.U64Digits.html)
- An iterator of `u64`digits representation of a`BigUint`or`BigInt`, ordered least significant digit first.
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformBigInt.html)- BigInt - `rand`
- The back-end implementing rand’s `UniformSampler``BigInt`
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformBigUint.html)- BigUint - `rand`
- The back-end implementing rand’s `UniformSampler``BigUint`

# BigUint in num_bigint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-bigint/^0.4.5/struct.BigUint.html

`pub struct BigUint { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A big unsigned integer type.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_bigint/biguint.rs.html#596-604)#### pub fn [from_bytes_be](https://docs.rs#method.from_bytes_be)(bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_bigint/biguint.rs.html#596-604)

#### pub fn [from_bytes_be](https://docs.rs#method.from_bytes_be)(bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

Creates and initializes a [ BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html).

The bytes are in big-endian byte order.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use num_bigint::BigUint;
assert_eq!(BigUint::from_bytes_be(b"A"),
           BigUint::parse_bytes(b"65", 10).unwrap());
assert_eq!(BigUint::from_bytes_be(b"AA"),
           BigUint::parse_bytes(b"16705", 10).unwrap());
assert_eq!(BigUint::from_bytes_be(b"AB"),
           BigUint::parse_bytes(b"16706", 10).unwrap());
assert_eq!(BigUint::from_bytes_be(b"Hello world!"),
           BigUint::parse_bytes(b"22405534230753963835153736737", 10).unwrap());
```
Creates and initializes a [ BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html). The input slice must contain
ascii/utf8 characters in [0-9a-zA-Z].

`radix` must be in the range `2...36`.The function `from_str_radix` from the `Num` trait provides the same logic
for `&str` buffers.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use num_bigint::{BigUint, ToBigUint};
assert_eq!(BigUint::parse_bytes(b"1234", 10), ToBigUint::to_biguint(&1234));
assert_eq!(BigUint::parse_bytes(b"ABCD", 16), ToBigUint::to_biguint(&0xABCD));
assert_eq!(BigUint::parse_bytes(b"G", 16), None);
```
Creates and initializes a [ BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html). Each

`u8` of the input slice is
interpreted as one digit of the number
and must therefore be less than `radix`.The bytes are in big-endian byte order.
`radix` must be in the range `2...256`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use num_bigint::{BigUint};
let inbase190 = &[15, 33, 125, 12, 14];
let a = BigUint::from_radix_be(inbase190, 190).unwrap();
assert_eq!(a.to_radix_be(190), inbase190);
```
Creates and initializes a [ BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html). Each

`u8` of the input slice is
interpreted as one digit of the number
and must therefore be less than `radix`.The bytes are in little-endian byte order.
`radix` must be in the range `2...256`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```

let a = BigUint::from_radix_be(inbase190, 190).unwrap();
assert_eq!(a.to_radix_be(190), inbase190);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_bigint/biguint.rs.html#802-806)#### pub fn [to_str_radix](https://docs.rs#method.to_str_radix)(&self, radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_bigint/biguint.rs.html#802-806)

#### pub fn [to_str_radix](https://docs.rs#method.to_str_radix)(&self, radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

Returns the integer formatted as a string in the given radix.
`radix` must be in the range `2...36`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
use num_bigint::BigUint;
let i = BigUint::parse_bytes(b"ff", 16).unwrap();
assert_eq!(i.to_str_radix(16), "ff");
```
Returns the integer in the requested base in big-endian digit order.
The output is not given in a human readable alphabet but as a zero
based `u8` number.
`radix` must be in the range `2...256`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
use num_bigint::BigUint;
assert_eq!(BigUint::from(0xFFFFu64).to_radix_be(159),
           vec![2, 94, 27]);
// 0xFFFF = 65535 = 2*(159^2) + 94*159 + 27
```
Returns the integer in the requested base in little-endian digit order.
The output is not given in a human readable alphabet but as a zero
based u8 number.
`radix` must be in the range `2...256`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
use num_bigint::BigUint;
assert_eq!(BigUint::from(0xFFFFu64).to_radix_le(159),
           vec![27, 94, 2]);
// 0xFFFF = 65535 = 27 + 94*159 + 2*(159^2)
```
Returns `(self ^ exponent) % modulus`.

Panics if the modulus is zero.

Returns the modular multiplicative inverse if it exists, otherwise `None`.

This solves for `x` in the interval `[0, modulus)` such that `self * x ≡ 1 (mod modulus)`.
The solution exists if and only if `gcd(self, modulus) == 1`.

```
use num_bigint::BigUint;
use num_traits::{One, Zero};
let m = BigUint::from(383_u32);
// Trivial cases
assert_eq!(BigUint::zero().modinv(&m), None);
assert_eq!(BigUint::one().modinv(&m), Some(BigUint::one()));
let neg1 = &m - 1u32;
assert_eq!(neg1.modinv(&m), Some(neg1));
let a = BigUint::from(271_u32);
let x = a.modinv(&m).unwrap();
assert_eq!(x, BigUint::from(106_u32));
assert_eq!(x.modinv(&m).unwrap(), a);
assert!((a * x % m).is_one());
```

# BigInt in num_bigint - Rust

`pub struct BigInt { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A big signed integer type.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_bigint/bigint.rs.html#634-636)#### pub fn [from_bytes_be](https://docs.rs#method.from_bytes_be)(sign: [Sign](https://docs.rs/enum.Sign.html), bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_bigint/bigint.rs.html#634-636)

#### pub fn [from_bytes_be](https://docs.rs#method.from_bytes_be)(sign: [Sign](https://docs.rs/enum.Sign.html), bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

Creates and initializes a [ BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html).

The bytes are in big-endian byte order.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use num_bigint::{BigInt, Sign};
assert_eq!(BigInt::from_bytes_be(Sign::Plus, b"A"),
           BigInt::parse_bytes(b"65", 10).unwrap());
assert_eq!(BigInt::from_bytes_be(Sign::Plus, b"AA"),
           BigInt::parse_bytes(b"16705", 10).unwrap());
assert_eq!(BigInt::from_bytes_be(Sign::Plus, b"AB"),
           BigInt::parse_bytes(b"16706", 10).unwrap());
assert_eq!(BigInt::from_bytes_be(Sign::Plus, b"Hello world!"),
           BigInt::parse_bytes(b"22405534230753963835153736737", 10).unwrap());
```
Creates and initializes a [ BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html). Each

`u8` of the input slice is
interpreted as one digit of the number
and must therefore be less than `radix`.The bytes are in big-endian byte order.
`radix` must be in the range `2...256`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use num_bigint::{BigInt, Sign};
let inbase190 = vec![15, 33, 125, 12, 14];
let a = BigInt::from_radix_be(Sign::Minus, &inbase190, 190).unwrap();
assert_eq!(a.to_radix_be(190), (Sign:: Minus, inbase190));
```
Creates and initializes a [ BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html). Each

`u8` of the input slice is
interpreted as one digit of the number
and must therefore be less than `radix`.The bytes are in little-endian byte order.
`radix` must be in the range `2...256`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use num_bigint::{BigInt, Sign};
let inbase190 = vec![14, 12, 125, 33, 15];
let a = BigInt::from_radix_be(Sign::Minus, &inbase190, 190).unwrap();
assert_eq!(a.to_radix_be(190), (Sign::Minus, inbase190));
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_bigint/bigint.rs.html#872-881)#### pub fn [to_str_radix](https://docs.rs#method.to_str_radix)(&self, radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

#### pub fn [to_str_radix](https://docs.rs#method.to_str_radix)(&self, radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

Returns the integer formatted as a string in the given radix.
`radix` must be in the range `2...36`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
use num_bigint::BigInt;
let i = BigInt::parse_bytes(b"ff", 16).unwrap();
assert_eq!(i.to_str_radix(16), "ff");
```
Returns the integer in the requested base in big-endian digit order.
The output is not given in a human readable alphabet but as a zero
based `u8` number.
`radix` must be in the range `2...256`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
use num_bigint::{BigInt, Sign};
assert_eq!(BigInt::from(-0xFFFFi64).to_radix_be(159),
           (Sign::Minus, vec![2, 94, 27]));
// 0xFFFF = 65535 = 2*(159^2) + 94*159 + 27
```
Returns the integer in the requested base in little-endian digit order.
The output is not given in a human readable alphabet but as a zero
based `u8` number.
`radix` must be in the range `2...256`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
use num_bigint::{BigInt, Sign};
assert_eq!(BigInt::from(-0xFFFFi64).to_radix_le(159),
           (Sign::Minus, vec![27, 94, 2]));
// 0xFFFF = 65535 = 27 + 94*159 + 2*(159^2)
```
Returns the magnitude of the [ BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html) as a

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

```
use num_bigint::{BigInt, BigUint};
use num_traits::Zero;
assert_eq!(BigInt::from(1234).magnitude(), &BigUint::from(1234u32));
assert_eq!(BigInt::from(-4321).magnitude(), &BigUint::from(4321u32));
assert!(BigInt::ZERO.magnitude().is_zero());
```

#### pub fn [checked_add](https://docs.rs#method.checked_add)(&self, v: &[BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)>

#### pub fn [checked_mul](https://docs.rs#method.checked_mul)(&self, v: &[BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_bigint/bigint.rs.html#1004-1009)

#### pub fn [checked_div](https://docs.rs#method.checked_div)(&self, v: &[BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)>

Returns `(self ^ exponent) mod modulus`

Note that this rounds like `mod_floor`, not like the `%` operator,
which makes a difference when given a negative `self` or `modulus`.
The result will be in the interval `[0, modulus)` for `modulus > 0`,
or in the interval `(modulus, 0]` for `modulus < 0`

Panics if the exponent is negative or the modulus is zero.

Returns the modular multiplicative inverse if it exists, otherwise `None`.

This solves for `x` such that `self * x ≡ 1 (mod modulus)`.
Note that this rounds like `mod_floor`, not like the `%` operator,
which makes a difference when given a negative `self` or `modulus`.
The solution will be in the interval `[0, modulus)` for `modulus > 0`,
or in the interval `(modulus, 0]` for `modulus < 0`,
and it exists if and only if `gcd(self, modulus) == 1`.

```
use num_bigint::BigInt;
use num_integer::Integer;
use num_traits::{One, Zero};
let m = BigInt::from(383);
// Trivial cases
assert_eq!(BigInt::zero().modinv(&m), None);
assert_eq!(BigInt::one().modinv(&m), Some(BigInt::one()));
let neg1 = &m - 1u32;
assert_eq!(neg1.modinv(&m), Some(neg1));
// Positive self and modulus
let a = BigInt::from(271);
let x = a.modinv(&m).unwrap();
assert_eq!(x, BigInt::from(106));
assert_eq!(x.modinv(&m).unwrap(), a);
assert_eq!((&a * x).mod_floor(&m), BigInt::one());
// Negative self and positive modulus
let b = -&a;
let x = b.modinv(&m).unwrap();
assert_eq!(x, BigInt::from(277));
assert_eq!((&b * x).mod_floor(&m), BigInt::one());
// Positive self and negative modulus
let n = -&m;
let x = a.modinv(&n).unwrap();
assert_eq!(x, BigInt::from(-277));
assert_eq!((&a * x).mod_floor(&n), &n + 1);
// Negative self and modulus
let x = b.modinv(&n).unwrap();
assert_eq!(x, BigInt::from(-106));
assert_eq!((&b * x).mod_floor(&n), &n + 1);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_bigint/bigint.rs.html#1106-1108)#### pub fn [trailing_zeros](https://docs.rs#method.trailing_zeros)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_bigint/bigint.rs.html#1106-1108)

#### pub fn [trailing_zeros](https://docs.rs#method.trailing_zeros)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)>

Returns the number of least-significant bits that are zero,
or `None` if the entire number is zero.

Returns whether the bit in position `bit` is set,
using the two’s complement for negative numbers

Sets or clears the bit in the given position, using the two’s complement for negative numbers

Note that setting/clearing a bit (for positive/negative numbers, respectively) greater than the current bit length, a reallocation may be needed to store the new digits

# Arbitrary in arbitrary - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arbitrary/1.4.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html

    // Required method

    fn [arbitrary_take_rest](https://docs.rs#method.arbitrary_take_rest)(u: [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self> { ... }

    ) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>), [MaxRecursionReached](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)> { ... }
}## Expand description

Generate arbitrary structured values from raw, unstructured data.

The `Arbitrary` trait allows you to generate valid structured values, like
`HashMap`s, or ASTs, or `MyTomlConfig`, or any other data structure from
raw, unstructured bytes provided by a fuzzer.

[§](https://docs.rs#deriving-arbitrary)Deriving `Arbitrary`

Automatically deriving the `Arbitrary` trait is the recommended way to
implement `Arbitrary` for your types.

Using the custom derive requires that you enable the `"derive"` cargo
feature in your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
arbitrary = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
```
Then, you add the `#[derive(Arbitrary)]` annotation to your `struct` or
`enum` type definition:

```
use arbitrary::Arbitrary;
use std::collections::HashSet;
#[derive(Arbitrary)]
pub struct AddressBook {
    friends: HashSet<Friend>,
}
#[derive(Arbitrary, Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub enum Friend {
    Buddy { name: String },
    Pal { age: usize },
}
```
Every member of the `struct` or `enum` must also implement `Arbitrary`.

It is also possible to change the default bounds added by the derive:

```
use arbitrary::Arbitrary;
trait Trait {
    type Assoc: for<'a> Arbitrary<'a>;
}
#[derive(Arbitrary)]
// The bounds are used verbatim, so any existing trait bounds will need to be repeated.
#[arbitrary(bound = "T: Trait")]
struct Point<T: Trait> {
    x: T::Assoc,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-arbitrary-by-hand)Implementing `Arbitrary` By Hand

Implementing `Arbitrary` mostly involves nested calls to other `Arbitrary`
arbitrary implementations for each of your `struct` or `enum`’s members. But
sometimes you need some amount of raw data, or you need to generate a
variably-sized collection type, or something of that sort. The
[ Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html) type helps you with these tasks.

```
use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Result, Unstructured};
impl<'a, T> Arbitrary<'a> for MyCollection<T>
where
    T: Arbitrary<'a>,
{
    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
        // Get an iterator of arbitrary `T`s.
        let iter = u.arbitrary_iter::<T>()?;
        // And then create a collection!
        let mut my_collection = MyCollection::new();
        for elem_result in iter {
            let elem = elem_result?;
            my_collection.insert(elem);
        }
        Ok(my_collection)
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#a-note-on-output-distributions)A Note On Output Distributions

There is no requirement for a particular distribution of the values. For
example, it is not required that every value appears with the same
probability. That being said, the main use for `Arbitrary` is for fuzzing,
so in many cases a uniform distribution will make the most sense in order to
provide the best coverage of the domain. In other cases this is not
desirable or even possible, for example when sampling from a uniform
distribution is computationally expensive or in the case of collections that
may grow indefinitely.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#207)#### fn [arbitrary](https://docs.rs#tymethod.arbitrary)(u: &mut [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#207)

#### fn [arbitrary](https://docs.rs#tymethod.arbitrary)(u: &mut [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

Generate an arbitrary value of `Self` from the given unstructured data.

Calling `Arbitrary::arbitrary` requires that you have some raw data,
perhaps given to you by a fuzzer like AFL or libFuzzer. You wrap this
raw data in an `Unstructured`, and then you can call `<MyType as Arbitrary>::arbitrary` to construct an arbitrary instance of `MyType`
from that unstructured data.

Implementations may return an error if there is not enough data to
construct a full instance of `Self`, or they may fill out the rest of
`Self` with dummy values. Using dummy values when the underlying data is
exhausted can help avoid accidentally “defeating” some of the fuzzer’s
mutations to the underlying byte stream that might otherwise lead to
interesting runtime behavior or new code coverage if only we had just a
few more bytes. However, it also requires that implementations for
recursive types (e.g. `struct Foo(Option<Box<Foo>>)`) avoid infinite
recursion when the underlying data is exhausted.

```
use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Unstructured};
#[derive(Arbitrary)]
pub struct MyType {
    // ...
}
// Get the raw data from the fuzzer or wherever else.
let raw_data: &[u8] = get_raw_data_from_fuzzer();
// Wrap that raw data in an `Unstructured`.
let mut unstructured = Unstructured::new(raw_data);
// Generate an arbitrary instance of `MyType` and do stuff with it.
if let Ok(value) = MyType::arbitrary(&mut unstructured) {
    do_stuff(value);
}
```
See also the documentation for [ Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html).

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#216-218)#### fn [arbitrary_take_rest](https://docs.rs#method.arbitrary_take_rest)(u: [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#216-218)

#### fn [arbitrary_take_rest](https://docs.rs#method.arbitrary_take_rest)(u: [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

Generate an arbitrary value of `Self` from the entirety of the given
unstructured data.

This is similar to Arbitrary::arbitrary, however it assumes that it is
the last consumer of the given data, and is thus able to consume it all
if it needs.  See also the documentation for
[ Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html).

Get a size hint for how many bytes out of an `Unstructured` this type
needs to construct itself.

This is useful for determining how many elements we should insert when creating an arbitrary collection.

The return value is similar to [ Iterator::size_hint](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html#method.size_hint): it returns a
tuple where the first element is a lower bound on the number of bytes
required, and the second element is an optional upper bound.

The default implementation return `(0, None)` which is correct for any
type, but not ultimately that useful. Using `#[derive(Arbitrary)]` will
create a better implementation. If you are writing an `Arbitrary`
implementation by hand, and your type can be part of a dynamically sized
collection (such as `Vec`), you are strongly encouraged to override this
default with a better implementation, and also override
[ try_size_hint](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.try_size_hint).

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-implement-this)How to implement this

If the size hint calculation is a trivial constant and does not recurse
into any other `size_hint` call, you should implement it in `size_hint`:

```
use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, Result, Unstructured};
struct SomeStruct(u8);
impl<'a> Arbitrary<'a> for SomeStruct {
    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
        let buf = &mut [0];
        u.fill_buffer(buf)?;
        Ok(SomeStruct(buf[0]))
    }
    #[inline]
    fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
        let _ = depth;
        (1, Some(1))
    }
}
```
Otherwise, it should instead be implemented in [ try_size_hint](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.try_size_hint),
and the

`size_hint` implementation should forward to it:```
use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, MaxRecursionReached, Result, Unstructured};
struct SomeStruct<A, B> {
    a: A,
    b: B,
}
impl<'a, A: Arbitrary<'a>, B: Arbitrary<'a>> Arbitrary<'a> for SomeStruct<A, B> {
    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
        // ...
    }
    fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
        // Return the value of try_size_hint
        //
        // If the recursion fails, return the default, always valid `(0, None)`
        Self::try_size_hint(depth).unwrap_or_default()
    }
    fn try_size_hint(depth: usize) -> Result<(usize, Option<usize>), MaxRecursionReached> {
        // Protect against potential infinite recursion with
        // `try_recursion_guard`.
        size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth, |depth| {
            // If we aren't too deep, then `recursion_guard` calls
            // this closure, which implements the natural size hint.
            // Don't forget to use the new `depth` in all nested
            // `try_size_hint` calls! We recommend shadowing the
            // parameter, like what is done here, so that you can't
            // accidentally use the wrong depth.
            Ok(size_hint::and(
                <A as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
                <B as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
            ))
        })
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#invariant)Invariant

It must be possible to construct every possible output using only inputs
of lengths bounded by these parameters. This applies to both
[ Arbitrary::arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#tymethod.arbitrary) and

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.arbitrary_take_rest)

`Arbitrary::arbitrary_take_rest`This is trivially true for `(0, None)`. To restrict this further, it
must be proven that all inputs that are now excluded produced redundant
outputs which are still possible to produce using the reduced input
space.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#423-425)#### fn [try_size_hint](https://docs.rs#method.try_size_hint)(
    depth: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>), [MaxRecursionReached](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#423-425)

#### fn [try_size_hint](https://docs.rs#method.try_size_hint)(
    depth: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>), [MaxRecursionReached](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)>

Get a size hint for how many bytes out of an `Unstructured` this type
needs to construct itself.

Unlike [ size_hint](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html), this function keeps the information that the
recursion limit was reached. This is required to “short circuit” the
calculation and avoid exponential blowup with recursive structures.

If you are implementing [ size_hint](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html) for a struct that could be
recursive, you should implement

`try_size_hint` and call the
`try_size_hint` when recursingThe return value is similar to [ core::iter::Iterator::size_hint](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html#method.size_hint): it
returns a tuple where the first element is a lower bound on the number
of bytes required, and the second element is an optional upper bound.

The default implementation returns the value of [ size_hint](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html) which is
correct for any type, but might lead to exponential blowup when dealing
with recursive types.

[§](https://docs.rs#invariant-1)Invariant

It must be possible to construct every possible output using only inputs
of lengths bounded by these parameters. This applies to both
[ Arbitrary::arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#tymethod.arbitrary) and

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.arbitrary_take_rest)

`Arbitrary::arbitrary_take_rest`This is trivially true for `(0, None)`. To restrict this further, it
must be proven that all inputs that are now excluded produced redundant
outputs which are still possible to produce using the reduced input
space.

[§](https://docs.rs#when-to-implement-try_size_hint)When to implement `try_size_hint`

If you 100% know that the type you are implementing `Arbitrary` for is
not a recursive type, or your implementation is not transitively calling
any other `size_hint` methods, you may implement [ size_hint](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html), and the
default

`try_size_hint` implementation will use it.Note that if you are implementing `Arbitrary` for a generic type, you
cannot guarantee the lack of type recursion!

Otherwise, when there is possible type recursion, you should implement
`try_size_hint` instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-depth-parameter)The `depth` parameter

When implementing `try_size_hint`, you need to use
[ arbitrary::size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth)](https://docs.rs/size_hint/fn.try_recursion_guard.html)
to prevent potential infinite recursion when calculating size hints for
potentially recursive types:

```
use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, MaxRecursionReached, Unstructured};
// This can potentially be a recursive type if `L` or `R` contain
// something like `Box<Option<MyEither<L, R>>>`!
enum MyEither<L, R> {
    Left(L),
    Right(R),
}
impl<'a, L, R> Arbitrary<'a> for MyEither<L, R>
where
    L: Arbitrary<'a>,
    R: Arbitrary<'a>,
{
    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured) -> arbitrary::Result<Self> {
        // ...
    }
    fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
        // Return the value of `try_size_hint`
        //
        // If the recursion fails, return the default `(0, None)` range,
        // which is always valid.
        Self::try_size_hint(depth).unwrap_or_default()
    }
    fn try_size_hint(depth: usize) -> Result<(usize, Option<usize>), MaxRecursionReached> {
        // Protect against potential infinite recursion with
        // `try_recursion_guard`.
        size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth, |depth| {
            // If we aren't too deep, then `recursion_guard` calls
            // this closure, which implements the natural size hint.
            // Don't forget to use the new `depth` in all nested
            // `try_size_hint` calls! We recommend shadowing the
            // parameter, like what is done here, so that you can't
            // accidentally use the wrong depth.
            Ok(size_hint::or(
                <L as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
                <R as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
            ))
        })
    }
}
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Serialize in serde_core::ser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html

```
pub trait Serialize {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[serialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize)<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<S::[Ok](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), S::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where S: [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html);
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be serialized into any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Serialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/index.html). All of
these can be serialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [ serde_derive](https://crates.io/crates/serde_derive) to
automatically generate

`Serialize` implementations for structs and enums in
your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html)for how to use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Serialize` manually for some
type in your program. See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the
manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Serialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the [ linked-hash-map](https://crates.io/crates/linked-hash-map) crate provides a

[type that is serializable by Serde because the crate provides an implementation of](https://docs.rs/linked-hash-map/*/linked_hash_map/struct.LinkedHashMap.html)

`LinkedHashMap<K, V>``Serialize` for it.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize this value into the given Serde serializer.

See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the manual for more
information about how to implement this method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
// This is what #[derive(Serialize)] would generate.
impl Serialize for Person {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut s = serializer.serialize_struct("Person", 3)?;
        s.serialize_field("name", &self.name)?;
        s.serialize_field("age", &self.age)?;
        s.serialize_field("phones", &self.phones)?;
        s.end()
    }
}
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

## Implementations on Foreign Types[§](https://docs.rs#foreign-impls)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/impls.rs.html#397-402)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-(T,))### impl<T> [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html) for [(T₁, T₂, …, Tₙ)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.tuple.html#trait-implementations-1)

This trait is implemented for tuples up to 16 items long.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/impls.rs.html#397-402)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-(T,))

### impl<T> [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html) for [(T₁, T₂, …, Tₙ)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.tuple.html#trait-implementations-1)

This trait is implemented for tuples up to 16 items long.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/impls.rs.html#492-504)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-Rc%3CT%3E)Available on **crate feature **`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`) only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/impls.rs.html#492-504)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-Rc%3CT%3E)

**crate feature**only.

`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`)Serializing a data structure containing `Rc` will serialize a copy of
the contents of the `Rc` each time the `Rc` is referenced within the
data structure. Serialization will not attempt to deduplicate these
repeated data.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/impls.rs.html#506-518)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-Arc%3CT%3E)Available on **crate feature **`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`) only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/impls.rs.html#506-518)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-Arc%3CT%3E)

**crate feature**only.

`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`)Serializing a data structure containing `Arc` will serialize a copy of
the contents of the `Arc` each time the `Arc` is referenced within the
data structure. Serialization will not attempt to deduplicate these
repeated data.

# Deserialize in serde_core::de - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html

`pub trait Deserialize<'de>: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [deserialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.deserialize)<D>(deserializer: D) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, D::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where D: [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)<'de>;
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be deserialized from any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Deserialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/index.html). All of these
can be deserialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called `serde_derive` to
automatically generate `Deserialize` implementations for structs and enums
in your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html) for how to
use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Deserialize` manually for
some type in your program. See the [Implementing
 Deserialize](https://serde.rs/impl-deserialize.html) section of the manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Deserialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the `linked-hash-map` crate provides a
`LinkedHashMap<K, V>` type that is deserializable by Serde because the crate
provides an implementation of `Deserialize` for it.

[§](https://docs.rs#lifetime)Lifetime

The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
borrowed by `Self` when deserialized. See the page [Understanding
deserializer lifetimes](https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html) for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

}## Expand description

Helper trait handling actual uniform sampling.

See the [module documentation](https://docs.rs/index.html) on how to implement [ Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html) range
sampling for a custom type.

Implementation of [ sample_single](https://docs.rs/trait.UniformSampler.html#method.sample_single) is optional, and is only useful when
the implementation can be faster than

`Self::new(low, high).sample(rng)`.## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Construct self, with inclusive lower bound and exclusive upper bound
`[low, high)`.

Usually users should not call this directly but instead use
`Uniform::new`, which asserts that `low < high` before calling this.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand/distributions/uniform.rs.html#248-251)#### fn [new_inclusive](https://docs.rs#tymethod.new_inclusive)<B1, B2>(low: B1, high: B2) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand/distributions/uniform.rs.html#248-251)

#### fn [new_inclusive](https://docs.rs#tymethod.new_inclusive)<B1, B2>(low: B1, high: B2) -> Self

Construct self, with inclusive bounds `[low, high]`.

Usually users should not call this directly but instead use
`Uniform::new_inclusive`, which asserts that `low <= high` before
calling this.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Sample a single value uniformly from a range with inclusive lower bound
and exclusive upper bound `[low, high)`.

By default this is implemented using
`UniformSampler::new(low, high).sample(rng)`. However, for some types
more optimal implementations for single usage may be provided via this
method (which is the case for integers and floats).
Results may not be identical.

Note that to use this method in a generic context, the type needs to be
retrieved via `SampleUniform::Sampler` as follows:

```
use rand::{thread_rng, distributions::uniform::{SampleUniform, UniformSampler}};
fn sample_from_range<T: SampleUniform>(lb: T, ub: T) -> T {
    let mut rng = thread_rng();
    <T as SampleUniform>::Sampler::sample_single(lb, ub, &mut rng)
}
```

    high: B2,
    rng: [&mut R](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
) -> Self::[X](https://docs.rs/trait.UniformSampler.html#associatedtype.X)

# num-complex

 = "0.4"
 = false

enabled. Where possible, `FloatCore` is used instead.  Formatting complex
